CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT, 1987 Constitution Act, 1867
1.	The Constitution Act, 1867 is amended by adding thereto, immediately after section 1 thereof, the following section:
"2. (1) The Constitution of Canada shall be interpreted in a manner consistent with
(a)	the recognition that the existence of French-speaking Canadians, centred in Quebec but also present elsewhere in Canada, and Englishspeaking Canadians, concentrated outside Quebec but also present in Quebec, constitutes a fundamental characteristic of Canada; and
(b)	the recognition that Quebec constitutes within Canada a distinct
society.
(2)	The role of the Parliament of Canada and the provincial legislatures to preserve the fundamental characteristic of Canada referred to in paragraph (l)(a) is affirmed.
(3)	The role of the legislature and Government of Quebec to preserve and promote the distinct identity of Quebec referred to in paragraph (l)(b) is affirmed.
(4)	Nothing in this section derogates from the powers, rights or privileges of Parliament or the Government of Canada, or of the legislatures or governments of the provinces, including any powers, rights or privileges relating to language."
2.	The said Act is further amended by adding thereto, immediately after section 24 thereof, the following section:
"25. (1) Where a vacancy occurs in the Senate, the government of the province to which the vacancy relates may, in relation to that vacancy, submit to the Queen's Privy Council for Canada the names of persons who may be summoned to the Senate.
(2)	Until an amendment to the Constitution of Canada is made in relation to the Senate pursuant to section 41 of the Constitution Act, 1982, the person summoned to Fill a vacancy in the Senate shall be chosen from among persons whose names have been submitted under subsection (1) by the government of the province to which the vacancy relates and must be acceptable to the Queen's Privy Council for Canada."
3.	The said Act is further amended by adding thereto, immediately after section 95 thereof, the following heading and sections:
"Agreements on Immigration and Aliens
95A. The Government of Canada shall, at the request of the government of any province, negotiate with the government of that province for the purpose of concluding an agreement relating to immigration or the temporary admission of aliens into that province that is appropriate to the needs and circumstances of that province.
95B. (1) Any agreement concluded between Canada and a province in relation to immigration or the temporary admission of aliens into that province has the force of law from the time it is declared to do so in accordance with subsection 95C(1) and shall from that time have effect notwithstanding class 25 of section 91 or section 95.
(2)	An agreement that has the force of law under subsection (1) shall have effect only so long and so far as it is not repugnant to any provision of an Act of the Parliament of Canada that sets national standards and objectives relating to immigration or aliens, including any provision that establishes general classes of immigrants or relates to levels of immigration for Canada or that prescribes classes of individuals who are inadmissible into Canada.
(3)	The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms applies in respect of any agreement that has the force of law under subsection (1) and in respect of anything done by the Parliament or Government of Canada, or the legislature or government of a province, pursuant to any such agreement.
95C. (1) A declaration that an agreement referred to in subsection 95B( 1) has the force of law may be made by proclamation issued by the Governor General under the Great Seal of Canada only where so authorized by resolutions of the Senate and House of Commons and of the legislative assembly of the province that is a party to the agreement.
(2) An amendment to an agreement referred to in subsection 95B(1) may be made by proclamation issued by the Governor General under the Great Seal of Canada only where so authorized
(a)	by resolutions of the Senate and House of Commons and of the
legislative assembly of the province that is a party to the agreement; or
(b)	in such other manner as is set out in the agreement.

October 2, 1987
Constitutional Amendments, 1987
95D. Sections 46 to 48 of the Constitution Act, 1982 apply, with such modifications as the circumstances require, in respect of any declaration made pursuant to subsection 95C( 1), any amendment to an agreement made pursuant to subsection 95C(2) or any amendment made pursuant to section 95E.
95E. An amendment to sections 95A to 95D or this section may be made in accordance with the procedure set out in subsection 38(1) of the Constitution Act, 1982, but only if the amendment is authorized by resolutions of the legislative assemblies of all the provinces that are, at the time of the amendment, parties to an agreement that has the force of law under subsection 95B( 1)."
4.	The said Act is further amended by adding thereto, immediately preceding section 96 thereof, the following heading:
"General"
5.	The said Act is further amended by adding thereto, immediately preceding section 101 thereof, the following heading:
"Courts Established by the Parliament of Canada"
6.	The said Act is further amended by adding thereto, immediately after section 101 thereof, the following heading and sections:
"Supreme Court of Canada
101 A. (1) The court existing under the name of the Supreme Court of Canada is hereby continued as the general court of appeal for Canada, and as an additional court for the better administration of the laws of Canada, and shall continue to be a superior court of record.
(2) The Supreme Court of Canada shall consist of a chief justice to be called the Chief Justice of Canada and eight other judges, who shall be appointed by the Governor General in Council by letters patent under the Great Seal.
101 B. (1) Any person may be appointed a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada who, after having been admitted to the bar of any province or territory, has, for a total of at least ten years, been a judge of any court in Canada or a member of the bar of any province or territory.
(2) At least three judges of the Supreme Court of Canada shall be appointed from among persons who, after having been admitted to the bar of Quebec, have, for a total of at least ten years, been judges of any court of Quebec or of any court established by the Parliament of Canada, or members of the bar of Quebec.
IOIC.	(1) Where a vacancy occurs in the Supreme Court of Canada, the government of each province may, in relation to that vacancy, submit to the Minister of Justice of Canada the names of any of the persons who have been admitted to the bar of that province and are qualified under section 101 B for appointment to that court.
(2)	Where an appointment is made to the Supreme Court of Canada, the Governor General in Council shall, except where the Chief Justice is appointed from among members of the Court, appoint a person whose name has been submitted under subsection (1) and who is acceptable to the Queen's Privy Council for Canada.
(3)	Where an appointment is made in accordance with subsection (2) of any of the three judges necessary to meet the requirement set out in subsection 101 B(2), the Governor General in Council shall appoint a person whose name has been submitted by the Government of Quebec.
(4)	Where an appointment is made in accordance with subsection (2) otherwise than as required under subsection (3), the Governor General in Council shall appoint a person whose name has been submitted by the government of a province other than Quebec.
IOID.	Sections 99 and 100 apply in respect of the judges of the Supreme Court of Canada.
101 E. (1) Sections 101A to 101D shall not be construed as abrogating or derogating from the powers of the Parliament of Canada to make laws under section 101 except to the extent that such laws are inconsistent with those sections.
(2) For greater certainty, section 101A shall not be construed as abrogating or derogating from the powers of the Parliament of Canada to make laws relating to the reference of questions of law or fact, or any other matters, to the Supreme Court of Canada."
7.	The said Act is further amended by adding thereto, immediately after section 106 thereof, the following section:
"106A. (1) The Government of Canada shall provide reasonable compensation to the government of a province that chooses not to participate in a national shared-cost program that is established by the
Government of Canada after the coming into force of this section in an area of exclusive provincial jurisdiction, if the province carries on a program or initiative that is compatible with the national objectives.
(2) Nothing in this section extends the legislative powers of the Parliament of Canada or of the legislatures of the provinces."
8.	The said Act is further amended by adding thereto the following heading and sections:
"XII-Conferences on the Economy and Other Matters
148.	A conference composed of the Prime Minister of Canada and the first ministers of the provinces shall be convened by the Prime Minister of Canada at least once each year to discuss the state of the Canadian economy and such other matters as may be appropriate.
XIII-References
149.	A reference to this Act shall be deemed to include a reference to any amendments thereto."
Constitution Act, 1982
9.	Sections 40 to 42 of the Constitution Act, 1982 are repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"40. Where an amendment is made under subsection 38(1) that transfers legislative powers from provincial legislatures to Parliament, Canada shall provide reasonable compensation to any province to which the amendment does not apply.
41. An amendment to the Constitution of Canada in relation to the following matters may be made by proclamation issued by the Governor General under the Great Seal of Canada only where authorized by resolutions of the Senate and House of Commons and of the legislative assembly of each province:
(a)	the office of the Queen, the Governor General and the Lieutenant Governor of a province;
(b)	the powers of the Senate and the method of selecting Senators;
(c)	the number of members by which a province is entitled to be represented in the Senate and the residence qualifications of Senators:
(d)	the right of a province to a number of members in the House of Commons not less than the number of Senators by which the province was entitled to be represented on April 17, 1982;
(e)	the principle of proportionate representation of the provinces in the House of Commons prescribed by the Constitution of Canada;
(f)	subject to section 43, the use of the English or the French language;
(g)	the Supreme Court of Canada;
(h)	the extension of existing provinces into the territories;
(i)	notwithstanding any other law or practice, the establishment of new provinces; and
(j)	an amendment to this Part."
10.	Section 44 of the said Act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"44. Subject to section 41, Parliament may exclusively make laws amending the Constitution of Canada in relation to the executive government of Canada or the Senate and House of Commons."
11.	Subsection 46(1) of the said Act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"46. (1) The procedures for amendment under sections 38, 41 and 43 may be initiated either by the Senate or the House of Commons or by the legislative assembly of a province."
12.	Subsection 47(1) of the said Act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"47. (1) An amendment to the Constitution of Canada made by proclamation under section 38, 41 or 43 may be made without a resolution of the Senate authorizing the issue of the proclamation if, within one hundred and eighty days after the adoption by the House of Commons of a resolution authorizing its issue, the Senate has not adopted such a resolution and if, at any time after the expiration of that period, the House of Commons again adopts the resolution."
13.	Part VI of the said Act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"Part VI
Constitutional Conferences
50. (1) A constitutional conference composed of the Prime Minister of Canada and the first ministers of the provinces shall be convened by the Prime Minister of Canada at least once each year, commencing in 1988.
October 2, 1987

(2) The conferences convened under subsection (1) shall have included on their agenda the following matters:
(a)	Senate reform, including the role and functions of the Senate, its powers, the method of selecting Senators and representation in the Senate;
(b)	roles and responsibilities in relation to fisheries; and
(c)	such other matters as are agreed upon."
14.	Subsection 52(2) of the said Act is amended by striking out the word "and" at the end of paragraph (b) thereof, by adding the word "and" at the end of paragraph (c) thereof and by adding thereto the following paragraph:
"(d) any other amendment to the Constitution of Canada."
15.	Section 61 of the said Act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"61. A reference to the Constitution Act 1982, or a reference to the Constitution Acts 1867 to 1982, shall be deemed to include a reference to any amendments thereto."
General
16.	Nothing in section 2 of the Constitution Act. 1867 affects section 25 or 27 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, section 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982 or class 24 of section 91 of the Constitution Act, 1867.
Citation
17.	This amendment may be cited as the Constitution Amendment, 1987.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased this morning to have the opportunity to share some thoughts with my colleagues in the House on the resolution before us, which is commonly known as the Meech Lake Accord, and on the amendments thereto.
I had the privilege during the past two months to attend about 90 per cent of the hearings of the joint committee on the Accord. Participating in those hearings was an educational process without parallel.
I was startled at times during the hearings at the enormous contrast in the appreciation of the Accord by different Canadians.
Perhaps I could summarize the hearings as follows: witnesses almost universally welcomed Quebec into the constitutional Canadian family. Second, witnesses generally endorsed the Accord but some were partisan to a particular view as to how the Accord affected them or their view of the shape of Canada's social and political make-up.
When learning that an Accord had been agreed on by the First Ministers in the evening of April 30, I recall being overwhelmed by a flood of emotion and pride that a pathway had been found to allow Quebec willingly to take its place in our constitutional confederation. It was a precious moment, long to be cherished and long to be remembered.
June 2 and June 3, 1987, were equally dramatic but to some extent anticlimactic. Looking back, I was never troubled by the distinct society clause in the Accord. I always felt that
Quebec was a distinct society and that view was reinforced by Jack Pickersgill when he related to the committee some of the history of the evolution of the Quebec society in North America, pointing out to us that certain things were granted to the French community in Canada back in 1760s, 1770s and through the 1790s, that related to their ability to practice the Catholic religion and other things relating to their language and civil law.
I could accept as well those procedures in the Accord which related to appointments of Senators and Supreme Court judges. If I had concerns after the Accord was signed, they related to the spending powers that were identified there and, to some extent, about the amending formula. I will return to the spending powers formula in a few moments, but before doing so, I would like to comment on some of the broader issues.
In a nutshell, the constitutional Accord, properly known as the Meech Lake agreement, is a three-prong consensus by Canada's First Ministers, to bring about Quebec's full and active participation in Canada's constitutional evolution, to foster greater harmony among Governments through new arrangements, and to hold annual constitutional conferences. In reviewing its finding and conclusions, the joint committee emphasized the nearly unanimous view of witnesses before it that Quebec rejoining the Canadian constitutional family is an important and desirable goal.
The question at hand, then, is whether the reform package negotiated by the First Ministers ultimately contributes to an improved Confederation for all Canadians. In passing judgment on the advisability of the agreement, the joint committee drew upon the wisdom of one of its testifying constitutional experts who argued that, given the importance of the success of the Accord as a package of constitutional reforms, any deficiencies it may contain must be seen to be serious and likely. While conceding that the Accord is a compromise, the joint committee's report asserts:
Nothing has been said to lead us to believe that the basic principles of the
Canadian Federation would be compromised.
That is, by the terms of the Accord. At the same time, the joint committee indicated that it heard a great body of opinion relating to matters which largely addressed constitutional problems outside the immediate confines of the Meech Lake agreement. In this vein, concerns with the operational issues of the Charter of Rights such as unsettled aboriginal matters and a lack of an institutional framework for constitutional discussions by First Ministers, figure prominently as problems which future constitutional conferences will have to, and must, address and resolve.
Allow me, Mr. Speaker, to return to my earlier concern about the spending power clause and how my thoughts and analysis evolved during the hearings. However, before doing so I would like to back up to the period of May and June of this
October 2, 1987

year. I was concerned, perhaps, that the spending powers would have some effect in balkanizing this tremendous Confederation of which we are privileged to be part. 1 recall the importance, going back to Confederation and the Confederation forefathers who put so much thought into our Confederation, of a strong central government. As we look at the report, the committee reminds us that innovation by provinces has historically been an important source of advances in social policy. Medicare is perhaps the most notable example. It became a national goal only after Saskatchewan showed that it could be done.
I do not, nor did the committee, discount the dangers of checkerboarding that goes beyond details and reaches fundamental objectives of social programs. If Canadians could not count on public services everywhere, it would inhibit provincial mobility and sap our sense of belonging to one nation, to one country and to one federation. I believe these concerns are nothing but phantoms. The Accord includes its own bulwarks against checkerboarding. One is clearly written into Section 106(a), so that it need not detain me long. It is the proviso that reasonable compensation is available only when provincial programs and initiatives are compatible with national objectives. I repeat "national objectives". It is this House that will always set the national objectives for Canada.
No compatibility, no money from the federal Treasury. That alone powerfully incites provinces to ensure compatibility if they do opt out of shared-cost programs. Nothing in that Constitutional Accord takes away from the power of this House to define its programs and to decide when it wants to spend money on matters of national importance.
A second bulwark, one that works in favour of co-operation, is the Accord's guarantee of First Ministers' conferences on the economy and other matters once a year. This provision has not attracted much attention during public and parliamentary discussion of the Accord. Perhaps we have become too blase and too easily take for granted the co-ordinating work done by First Ministers and the Prime Minister. The First Ministers' conference is a forum where the provinces can make their special concerns known so that federal programs are framed in ways that work for all Canadians wherever they live and whatever their social and economic setting. There is nothing in the Accord that compromises the authority of the federal Government to establish new national joint programs.
The Accord is intended to civilize the use of the spending power, and clarify that it cannot be used to oblige the provinces to take action in areas of exclusive provincial jurisdiction. The Accord also recognizes that it is constitutionally acceptable for Parliament to establish new shared-cost programs in areas of exclusive provincial jurisdiction, and provides that reasonable compensation will be granted to provincial Governments which establish a program or programs of initiative that are compatible with the national objective.
As I understand it, the reason the Accord addressed the federal spending power and the establishment of national
Constitutional Amendments, 1987
programs was to improve the bargaining relationship that results from the virtually unlimited federal spending power on the one hand and, on the other hand, the fact that its use in areas of exclusive provincial jurisdiction has sometimes led to federal provincial disagreements.
This question did not suddenly spring up in 1987. I would point out that the spending power was thoroughly examined by Governments in two previous exercises over the past many years, in 1968-1971, in the mid-1970s, and again in the period 1978-1979. I felt at times rebuffed by the intrusion of former Prime Minister Trudeau into the debate. However, in looking back, I found it was helpful because it did cause Canadians to focus in on some of the more important issues confronting us. But there was some dichotomy in what Mr. Trudeau said, not only in the public press but before the joint committee. It was a Government led by him in 1977 that gave up more constitutional power of spending in the block granting process to the provinces for health care and education than any Government in the history of this country since Confederation.
Where spending takes place over which this central Government has no control, at this point in our history and evolution, we have no guarantee, and have never had any, that funds that were to be directed for post-secondary education across this country would be spent for just that purpose.
The spending power clause found in the Accord is much simpler and more conducive to the establishment of new national social programs than the proposals the federal Government supported during those earlier exercises. It contains no consent mechanism, nor does it provide for unconditional compensation. Rather, it will encourage a healthier bargaining process between the two orders of Government and recognition that it is legitimate for Parliament to pursue joint economic and social programs on behalf of all Canadians.
Creative federalism was an idea that came up more than once at the committee's hearings. The group of 12 scholars, including Professors William Lederman, Peter Leslie, Richard Simeon and Donald Smiley, who submitted a joint brief, described the spending power provision as "the clearest embodiment of our view of creative federalism in the Accord". May I repeat that-the clearest embodiment of our view of creative federalism in the Accord.
We heard something very similar from J. W. Pickersgill, a veteran practitioner of government and a long-time Member of this House, when he met with the committee. Most Canadians want creative co-operation, Mr. Pickersgill said, and the acceptance of the Meech Lake Accord will make that possible. "I regard the Meech Lake Accord as the gate to greater unity and harmony in Canada," said Mr. Pickersgill. I agree with him. Negotiation is inseparable from federalism and creativity. It is essential to the harmonization of federal and provincial activity in a way that will translate into better policies for all.

October 2, 1987
Constitutional Amendments, 1987
So I agree with Mr. Pickersgill when he said, "Let us not shut the gate".
There were many touching moments during the presentations by the witnesses before the joint committee. I recall that very clever and enormously sharp advice that the committee received from many constitutional experts, some of whom had been involved with constitutional reform since the late 1930s and who brought an enormous amount of skill and advice- and good advice-to the committee about the value of the Accord.
I recall as well the very touching testimony by Madame Solange Chaput-Rolland, who appeared before the committee and who reviewed in considerable detail her historical perspective about the role the citizens of Quebec played in Confederation over the last 15 or 20 years. She spoke about the enormous emotion that was involved in the debate in 1979 and in 1980 as to whether or not Quebecers should stay within the constitutional framework of Canada. She spoke about the dichotomy between father and son, between mother and daughter, between neighbours, between communities. It was heart-wrenching. At those moments she had the committee in the palm of her hand, or at least she had me and I think most of my colleagues in the palm of her hand.
She spoke about the enormously gratifying feeling when Quebecers voted, not by an overwhelming but by a substantive majority, to stay within Confederation. She spoke as well with sincerity about the promises that were made to Quebecers by those who sat in this federal institution at that time, the promise that they would be brought into the greater Canadian constitutional family.
Then, she went on to review the process of 1980 and 1981, when a formula was put together to amend our Constitution and to bring it home, as it were, and to develop a framework, that the people from the Province of Quebec, Canadians with a great deal of generosity, talent and skill, were unable to support, that no political Party in the Province of Quebec was able to support. We heard her again say how enormously disappointed she was that she and her fellow citizens still had to sit outside, albeit morally, the Canadian Constitution. She reminded us, with tremendous emotion, of how she felt when the First Ministers came to an agreement about the Meech Lake Accord and its enormous importance to Canadians.
The joint committee not only gave its recommendation for adoption but it also stated, "It is neither necessary nor wise to recommend changes to the Accord at this time". As an alternate member of the joint committee, on September 9 I had the privilege of signing the report.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Are there questions or comments? The Lion. Member for Ottawa West (Mr. Daubney).

Mr. Speaker, I would like simply to congratulate my colleague on his excellent speech and on his important contribution to the work of the committee.
It was my pleasure to work with him just about every day during those long, hot days of August when we had the honour of reviewing the testimony and listening to the evidence that came before us from Canadians from all parts of this great country. I think the Hon. Member's survey of that evidence was very well done today. In fact, I think it has been one of the better contributions to this debate so far this week. It was an excellent, fair-minded survey, but also a very heartfelt one. I felt it expressed adequately the emotion he felt, the emotion we all felt, about the work that we were about.
I think it also served to underline a disappointment that we shared as members of the committee in hearing this excellent testimony, this positive testimony for the most part, from the constitutional experts and others from whom we heard, from right across Canada. He pointed out how badly we were served, I think quite frankly, by journalism in this country in the inadequate and, in some cases, distorted representation of that evidence in the press.
My friend from Nepean-Carleton dealt at some length, and very well, with the spending power. But I want him perhaps to comment, if he wishes, on some of the other evidence we had from people such as Gordon Robertson, who I believe he referred to in his remarks, the former Clerk of the Privy Council who, since the early 1950s, was the key constitutional adviser to federal Governments in this country. In fact the Trudeau Government was prepared to go much further than the Meech Lake Accord did, and in fact, as Mr. Robertson pointed out, there was no transfer of powers in this constitutional Accord of 1987, but the previous Liberal Government was prepared on several occasions to transfer federal power to the provinces.
I believe my hon. friend from Nepean-Carleton was sitting next to me when we had Mr. Trudeau before us that memorable night last August. When I asked Mr. Trudeau that question, I do not think he responded to it at all. But the record is clear, historically, that he was prepared, in fact, to transfer powers from the federal authority to the provincial authorities, something that is not done despite the misleading and shallow criticism which has been made about the Meech Lake constitutional Accord that is before the House at the present time. I would be glad if he would be prepared to comment on that.

I am very pleased to do so. By coincidence, I am happy that my colleague from Ottawa West (Mr. Daubney) actually focused in on the comments and advice of Gordon Robertson. I do so on that account with particular pleasure. For a long time Mr. Gordon Robertson was indirectly my boss in the sense that for a number of years he served as Chancellor of Carleton University where I had the privilege to be a professor.
One of the interesting things about Mr. Robertson's testimony was that he reminded the committee of his long
October 2, 1987

experience in constitutional matters wherein at times he had been the Government's chief adviser on constitutional reform, and at other times he had served as a consultant. As he reviewed the process of constitutional reform, particularly over the last 12 or 14 years, he was quick to point out to the committee that most of the items and the points of principle that are incorporated in the Accord had earlier been offered to the provinces by the Trudeau administration. Interestingly, that has never been denied, as I recall.
As we review our history, we find that the fact that one is prepared to place so much politics on something that is so lasting and fundamental to the peoples of Canada as its Constitution adds to the terrible dichotomy. We must work on the Constitution collectively to develop, refine and, in the course of time, make it more compatible to the needs of the great Confederation of which we are part.
In his presentation, Gordon Robertson clearly indicated to the committee that there was nothing in the Accord, as he saw it, that took away from the spending power of the central Government.
Let me say in closing, it is interesting to note that Mr. Robertson gave the joint committee the very strong advice that the Accord was indeed a dramatic and historic achievement that perhaps no other Government could have had the capability of putting together. It was his advice that the committee and Parliament endorse it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also wish to compliment the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Tupper) on the excellent speech that he delivered today on the Constitution and the steps forward that have been taken in terms of the Meech Lake Accord.
I represent one of the western regions, a different part of the country than those mentioned in the discussions that have been going on here this morning. One of the difficulties that we have always faced in the West was that we felt alienated. The process itself seemed to be somewhat alienating going back in the history of the constitutional talks and former leadership.
The very positive aspect that has taken place under the leadership of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is the change in terms of looking at the region. I was very pleased this morning to hear that in many ways I shared the thoughts of the Hon. Member for Ottawa West (Mr. Daubney) and the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton in terms of the uniting of this country. We feel in the region I represent that we have been alienated for years, and my own personal opinion is that this alienation has not been good for the uniting of Canada. Real steps have been taken under the leadership of the Prime Minister in bringing this country together, which is an absolutely outstanding achievement. I would like to hear the Member's comments from a central Canada point of view, as opposed to the region I represent in the West.

It is a treat for me to respond to my colleague from the Province of Saskatchewan. It is not often that I want
Constitutional Amendments, 1987
to give out a bouquet, or feel the need to do so to a colleague who may sit in the seats immediately to my right. For some time I felt that I wanted to compliment publicly the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom). During the time that he sat on the joint committee he showed an enormous amount of good judgment and a perspective on Canadian politics and Canadian problems, as well as practicality when attempting to point out to witnesses the strengths and weaknesses of the arguments that they were making at the particular point in time. This morning I wish to reinforce that compliment and say to the Hon. Member that I thought westerners were well represented in that dialogue.
Many Members in the House will know that my heritage is in Atlantic Canada. The Ottawa Valley has been my adopted home now for over a quarter of a century. I am one of those who historically has his roots in what one may refer to as Lower Canada. In fact my family was indirectly involved during 1863, 1864, and 1865 when my home province and Atlantic Canada struggled with the enormous debate on the pros and cons of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick joining Confederation with the Upper Canada provinces. In those days Nova Scotia was an enormously prosperous community. As time has moved forward economic disparities and political differences have developed. When one thinks about the tremendous nation we have in Atlantic Canada, Quebec and Ontario and the richness in so many ways of western Canada, there is absolutely no way that we can progress economically, socially, or constitutionally unless we are content with the way we will govern ourselves.
In this mechanism of 1987 we have taken a dramatic step forward in the construction of a truly Canadian family.

Mr. Speaker, it is my privilege to rise today and address the Meech Lake Accord, the constitutional agreement of 1987. I believe that there are few processes which highlight or better illustrate the difficulty of constitutional negotiations, and the difficulty of integrating negotiations of this nature between related parties into a democratic or quasi-democratic process of public approval.
Those of us who have participated in negotiations, be they commercial or labour-management, know that behind each negotiator lies a constituency. In many cases, the constituency does not approve or does not want the specific heads of negotiation that the negotiator may in time be impelled to accept. Indeed, there are times when negotiators accept things that they know will be unpopular in the cause of reaching an agreement which it is believed will hold wider implications for the good of the parties to the agreement.
It is also said somewhat tritely that a camel is a horse designed by a committee. Thus we see the shortcomings of the committee process. I believe that most of us in Canada are somewhat individualistic and are somewhat committed to

October 2, 1987
Constitutional Amendments, 1987
pursuing our own goals to a degree which sometimes impacts negatively on society but which nevertheless is a reflection of today's contemporary Canadian reality.
The flaws of the Meech Lake process unfortunately reflect not only the individualist orientation of our society but also the tendency within parliamentary government to invest full powers in the Government of the day, with only very limited consideration given to the views of an opposition at any level. Those flaws have been evidenced by some of the difficulties which the process of the Meech Lake Accord has encountered.
There was not the organized forum or public consultation before the signing of the agreement. We have, on the Prime Minister's authority in his televised speech announcing the Accord, the length, detail, and gravity of the constitutional consultations which preceded it. Nevertheless, I think it is fair to say that the Accord represents an agreement framed by, marketed to, and approved by the elected leadership of the country and the provinces, rather than something which arises from a nation-wide surge of public feeling and sentiment.
In the framing of the Meech Lake Accord there has obviously been difficulty and incompleteness in the identification of the potential problems, just as in 1982 the framers of that constitutional agreement failed to recognize the difficulties which the freedom of association clauses would cause for the organized labour movement, difficulties which must be resolved and which I believe strike by the exercise of one freedom against the exercise of another freedom in society.
The failure to identify the problems is not in any way a criticism of the work of the special joint committee. I should like to add briefly my thanks to that special joint committee for the excellent and indeed very hard work it put into its report. I think it is a document of considerable merit which illuminates the Meech Lake Accord for the benefit of all Canadians.
As has been said by many other speakers, the Constitution, after all, is a fundamental law. It underpins and bears up all other laws, yet it must be more than something chiselled in stone and exercised without exception or deviation. A successful Constitution can only be a living document or a living spirit, indeed, and in order to be successful it must be a people's document which is accessible and understandable by the people and which commands their broad loyalty and support.
As 1 said in the debate on June 11, it must be a document that reflects the inspirations from which our society springs and that reflects the aspirations of the people of our society. It is in this regard that written Constitutions encounter some difficulties. The complexity of the terminology of the Constitution is something that I would certainly recommend to the attention of future Governments, and, I suspect sadly, future generations.
The written Constitution is something that has been somewhat in vogue since the Constitution of the Haudenosanee
of the 17th century in the country. Indeed it is something of an irony that Great Britain, having itself no written constitution, imposed through the British North America Act a written Constitution on the Dominion of Canada.
There is much to be said in favour of the Meech Lake Accord; first and foremost, of course, the adhesion of the Province of Quebec.

So, Mr. Speaker, when I arrived in Canada as an immigrant I spent my first two years in Montreal, in the Province of Quebec, where I believe I was able to appreciate to some extent the constitutional, spiritual and emotional situation in which the people of Quebec found themselves. At the time certain Quebecers were motivated by a strong separatist leaning. There were obvious signs of tension within Quebec's society, as evidenced by acts of violence and the public debate which was carried on with an enthusiasm and a dedication the likes of which I never saw either before or after.
Mr. Speaker, to those who are against the Meech Lake Accord I can only say that perhaps they did not fully appreciate the nature of the very struggle of all segments of Quebec's society which went on during recent decades.

I would commend to those who have spoken against the Accord a profound study of the recent constitutional history of the Province of Quebec, because I think it is essential to an understanding of the importance of the agreement at which we are looking today.
The entrenchment of the Supreme Court in the Constitution is appropriate. The constitutionalization of the federal spending powers in areas of exclusive provincial jurisdiction is a necessary recognition in order to resolve a situation that has seen considerable tensions over the past few decades in which the federal Government has spent in areas in which the provinces, frankly, were not satisfied to see the federal Government intervening.
We have a minor reduction in the powers of the Senate concerning its ability to obstruct certain amendments for only 180 days, though there is much to be said against it so far as the Senate is concerned.
We have the freedom-and I believe it is not a threat to any part of the Canadian society-for provinces to make immigration agreements with the federal Government, not on a compulsory basis, not saying that agreements must be reached, but providing that opportunity. We have-and I think it was said by earlier speakers but bears repeating-the significance of an agreement among the 11 Premiers. I think the Hon. Member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Suluk) characterized it as an agreement between those who have not established a reputation for agreeing on very much, and I think he was perfectly right. The agreement itself represents a telling argument for the Accord, yet I must acknowledge that I also find fault with many aspects of the Meech Lake agreement.
October 2, 1987

I see the terminology or the framing of the agreement as a tragic and profound insult to the constitutional aspirations of our native people. It was not mentioned in the Meech Lake Accord that the talks on aboriginal self-government would be revived. There is no specific commitment to restarting those talks. Aboriginal peoples' legitimate and seriously held constitutional concerns were reduced to the level of other matters. I feel that that was a demeaning way in which to acknowledge the existence of those concerns.
Turning to the accolade of the distinct society, while I understand very well the necessity for stating that concept explictly with regard to the Province of Quebec, it was not conferred upon the equally and obviously distinct societies of our aboriginal nations. However, we must bear in mind and we must acknowledge that the entrenchment of self-government rights was not possible at Meech Lake because the participation of the aboriginal people was not invited and not foreseen in that type of discussion. While the aboriginal people of Canada have seen their sensibilities trampled on by the Meech Lake agreement, I believe they have not had any doors closed to them in their constitutional evolution. I will return later to the ways in which it can be clearly demonstrated that those doors remain open.
I should mention with pride the entrenchment of the aboriginal rights amendment in the 1982 agreement and my Party's pride in having participated in that.
Another obvious objection of mine to the Meech Lake Accord is the way in which it entrenches the role of the Senate. We first started on this slippery slide of giving constitutional legitimacy to a non-democratic, indeed an anti-democratic, institution in 1982. It has since been pointed out by learned constitutional scholars, including at least one in the Senate itself, that essentially the advent of the written Constitution by the 1982 Constitution Act gave the Senate powers that had not been envisaged as pertaining to that institution for a century or more. That was the gravest mistake of 1982.
Any agreement that envisages this non-democratic institution continuing to play a part within the democratic institutions of the Parliament and Government of Canada has got to have a great deal going for it before I can be persuaded to swallow the indignity of allowing 100 appointed Party faithful reaping their political reward to have a say in the legislation of this country.
With regard to the creation of provinces, I believe that the objections which my hon. colleague, the Member for Yukon (Ms. McLaughlin), has brought to this argument are very valid and well founded. Let us not forget that in 1905, Saskatchewan was inducted into the Confederation on the authority of the federal Government. The same happened in Newfoundland in 1949. However, from now on it will require an absolute majority of the provinces for any change in the structure to be made.
Constitutional Amendments, 1987
I beseech Hon. Members to think of the implications that that might bring with the change in demography of this country. Our country supports approximately 26 million people, but has the economic capacity to support 400 million to 700 million in the fullness of time. Yet we will, by this agreement, be binding ourselves to an arrangement which will enable the smallest province, whatever that might be 100 years from now, to unalterably obstruct the redivision, subdivision, or amalgamation of provinces which might seem appropriate to future generations.
It is also not clear under the Meech Lake agreement who controls the constitutional agenda. I believe the annual constitutional conference written into the Constitution itself is a serious mistake and almost a contradiction in terms because it implies that there will forever be constitutional business to regulate.
I wish to address the danger of alienating the excluded. We know very well the dangers that this country was placed in with the exclusion of the people of Quebec from full participation in the Constitution. Yet we must forever be vigilant against the possibility, indeed the probability, of excluding other groups by the operation of future constitutional amendments, including this Meech Lake Accord. There is very legitimate and deeply felt uncertainty as to the status of women's rights and the ability of native band Governments to deliver federal programs under the operation of the Meech Lake Accord. I have every confidence that they will be favourably resolved by the courts, but that, after all, is only one person's prediction.
The confusion and difficulty which the distinct identity clause has caused is also something which we must bear in mind in considering the Accord. There are other objections which have been brought by some which I do not believe have great force and effect but are worth mentioning.
I believe that the right of the provincial Governments to nominate to the Senate and the Supreme Court is not something which undermines federal institutions. In fact, it shows the confusion which exists in some minds with regard to what are national institutions and what are institutions of the Canadian federation. Let us not, after all, forget the paymaster factor. Let us not downgrade the intelligence, integrity or judgment of those who accept Supreme Court or even Senate appointments. Let us not accuse them of an inability to expand their presumed provincial perspective to the Canadian and national perspective.
One of the most telling factors in my assessment of the Meech Lake Accord has been the nature of the arguments put forward by those who oppose it. I must, with regret, say that I find them generally to be very deficient and in some cases deriving from an inspiration which I believe is not appropriate for the consideration of constitutional business in this country. Doubts have been raised about immigration. It has been said that there will be a general balkanization of the country. I do not see this happening. I endorse what the Leader of the

October 2, 1987
Ways and Means
Official Opposition has said. "I do not fear confrontation with the provinces. That is the inevitable nature of things in a federation."
Let us also note that, despite the imprecations of the former Prime Minister in what I can only consider to be a disgusting display of personalization of issues before the committee, the constitutional Accord is not simply addressing Quebec's asideness from the Constitution up until now. It is also addressing the phenomenon of western alienation, which has existed in this country and is addressed by the Meech Lake Accord.
It is not a question of there being a strong federal Government and a weak provincial Government, as Mr. Trudeau would have it. It is not a question, as critics would say, of there being strong provincial Governments and a weak federal Government under the Meech Lake Accord. We must remember that the adversarial model that this presupposes has never held sway in Canadian society. This shows a lack of appreciation of the degree of willingness and, frankly, the degree of skill at fashioning and implementing compromises, which I believe is inherent in the Canadian character.
The opposition to the Meech Lake Accord shows an imperfect understanding of the constitutional and historical perspective. None has effectively refuted the most telling evidence of Madam Chaput-Rolland. Until I hear that evidence refuted I cannot believe that a case has been made for the rejection of the Accord.
Those of us who came to this country as immigrants have experienced on a daily basis the generosity and openness of Canadian society to those whose origins are outside the country. We do not need a constitutional amendment to recognize that. We have that ongoing affirmation on a daily basis as do the aboriginal people of the country.
I believe that I may have a couple of minutes left when debate resumes. In deference to Question Period I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and all my colleagues for your consideration.

Mr. Speaker, the extent of child poverty, its destructiveness to the families involved, and the subsequent cost to society are not generally recognized in Canada. Nearly 30 per cent of Canadians living in poverty are under 16 years of age.
Members of Parliament have been invited to meet with a number of support groups next Tuesday to discuss the pressing problem of child poverty.
[DOT] (MOO)
Approximately one in five children lives in poverty; many are homeless and are forced to go to food banks. In recent years there has been a tremendous increase in single-parent families, a very high percentage of whom live in poverty.
The effects of poverty have been well documented by organizations concerned with its destructiveness on the lives of the poor. The stresses of poverty perpetuate more misery and contribute to the waste of human potential. Federal budgets since 1984 and proposals in the White Paper on Tax Reform, if implemented, will see child benefits reduced by $1.5 billion by 1991.
I call upon the Government to recognize the issue of child poverty now as changes are being contemplated to the tax and social security system, and to correct this socially unacceptable crisis which the Government has helped to create.

subtopic: FUTURE OF FIRESTONE PLANT IN HAMILTON
FUTURE OF FIRESTONE PLANT IN HAMILTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the witching hour is upon us. It is about time the federal Government did something to bring the two parties together to facilitate th? sale of Firestone to Cooper Tire. The Minister should know, though he probably will not because he has done
October 2, 1987

absolutely nothing on the dossier, that the two parties are only $5 million apart, but the word is if they do not come together very shortly, Firestone may pick up its machinery and equipment and silently steal off into the United States.
I call upon the Minister, again, as I have done in the past, as I have called upon the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), to show some leadership, to save those 1,400 jobs in the riding of Hamilton East, by going to Firestone in Akron, Ohio, directly. He knows that is where the decisions are being made.
Do not send civil servants. Show some political leadership, go to Akron and help save those jobs. Make Firestone realize that for $2 million we cannot afford to sacrifice 1,400 workers in Hamilton East.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF MINISTER OF STATE FOR SENIOR CITIZENS
APPOINTMENT OF MINISTER OF STATE FOR SENIOR CITIZENS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last August 27 the Prime Minister once again showed leadership by appointing the Minister of State (Seniors) (Mr. Hees), an appointment which was warmly welcomed, as evidenced by the applause and ovation given the Minister by all Parties in the House.
Quebec senior citizens were also very enthusiastic about the appointment. Among others, the Federation des aines dynamiques du Quebec issued a press release commending the Prime Minister for this historic initiative. They consider the Minister of State (Seniors) as, and I quote: An excellent choice as a Minister with whom we are quite prepared to cooperate.
Besides reacting enthusiastically to this appointment, the Federation des aines dynamiques du Quebec has expressed the hope that the provinces will draw inspiration from the Prime Minister's leadership and create similar ministries at the provincial level.
Mr. Speaker, that is yet another telling example of the importance this Government gives senior citizens, people who have generously contributed to the progress of our society. Our Government is aware that demographic evolution will translate into an ever aging population, and this is why we are moving with firmness and determination to give older Canadians the priority which they deserve.
Mr. Speaker, I am confident that under the leadership of the Minister of State (Seniors) older Canadians will be served with respect and understanding.

Mr. Speaker, the federal Government has added another notch to its plan to recover costs for most of its services at the expense of farmers and ultimately of consumers. We have seen this new user-pay philosophy put into place with farm improvement loans and small business loans. Now it is being extended to horticultural produce.
Previously, growers paid $5 per inspection to ensure that any fruits or vegetables shipped interprovincially met the designated grades so that consumers knew what they were buying and that they were getting good produce. Now the charge is being upped to three cents per hundredweight. The plan is to double it before next harvest and ultimately to quintuple it by 1990.
Potato producers in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick receiving a meagre six cents a pound now for their produce are particularly affected by this massive increase because they ship most of their spuds to other Canadian provinces. I call upon the Government to reconsider this new fee proposal.

Mr. Speaker, next week will be Canadian Family National Week. Unfortunately, in the last three years, families have been the group most neglected by the Conservative Government.
Everyone will recall the deindexing of family allowances. Everyone will recall the lowering of the maximum amount for the child tax credit. Everyone will recall the promise made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), a hand over his heart, swearing that there would be a child-care system for families, which are the corner stone of Canadian society. We have nothing yet.
Yesterday, we learned that the tax system is harder on large families. I invite all Canadian families to remember the three years of neglect of this Conservative Government and to do what it takes to defeat all Conservative Members of Parliament in Canada. These are the people who have neglected them.

October 2, 1987

Mr. Speaker, in an article in yesterday's Le Devoir, we learned from the eloquent pen of Michel Vastel that the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) had mounted a campaign to attract some of the provincial Liberals to federal politics, and we can now see why.
Mr. Speaker, I was astounded to read that article. The Liberals, with only 40 Members in this House, cannot agree on a single issue. Everything becomes a source of dissension among the Liberals. And what about their Leader, whose leadership is constantly being threatened? I believe that he should learn to lead his present followers before adding to his problems.
Mr. Speaker, the Liberals got Canadians used to confusion and incoherence, but they are now overdoing themselves and their leader is at the bottom of it.

subtopic: SHORTAGE OF HOUSES IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES
SHORTAGE OF HOUSES IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is presently a shortage of 2,400 houses in the Northwest Territories. Each year the need increases by approximately 150 houses just due to population growth.
According to a recent study, the population of the Northwest Territories grew by 14 per cent between 1981 and 1986 compared to 4 per cent for the entire country. At this rate of population growth, the housing shortage in the Northwest Territories will not be alleviated for at least 16 years.
The lack of funding for the application of Bill C-31, the legislation to reintegrate the native population to the Indian reserves, has amplified the problem of housing in the North. Sixty thousand claims for returns to the reserve, are still waiting to be processed.
The situation in the North will get worse. I urge the Government to increase immediately the number of units constructed through CMHC programs.

subtopic: NEW TIMMINS GOLD MINE-FINANCING RAISED BY FLOWTHROUGH SHARES
NEW TIMMINS GOLD MINE-FINANCING RAISED BY FLOWTHROUGH SHARES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had the pleasure on Wednesday to attend the opening of a new gold mine north of Timmins, Ontario. That mine, known as the Bell Creek Mine, owned by Canamex, is by world standards not a big mine. It will employ about 100 people, but 100 new jobs in Timmins are dramatically important.
In reality, those 100 jobs will translate into perhaps 300 or 400 jobs. Indeed, it was a proud moment for my colleague from Timmins-Chapleau.
A most significant highlight of this mine is that it was the first one in Canada to be discovered, developed and brought into production by financing raised by flow-through shares.
Normally at mine openings, the president of the company or the chairman of the board is praising the financiers for their help in bringing a new unit into production, but the situation was much different in Bell Creek on Wednesday. The president was praising the federal Government for its responsible and creative fiscal and tax policies that allowed the creation of this particular new wealth.
In the next year, this same company, Canamex, will be bringing three additional mines into production, all financed and created by this particular financing mechanism. It is a demonstration of what good fiscal policy can do.

[DOT] (mo)

Mr. Speaker, on September 22, Lamford Forest Products of Sooke, British Columbia, was presented with a Canada Award for Business Excellence in the labour/management category. The award is well deserved and highlights what can be accomplished through co-operative effort. In this instance, however, labour/management relations were simplified because at Lamford labour is management.
Two years ago Sooke Forest Products closed its lumber operation because the company was unable to operate financially. Rather than accept the end of their livelihood, the 270 I.W.A. members in Sooke established the employee-owned Lamford Forest Products. Today that operation is one of the most efficient high-recovery mills in North America, employing 275 shareholders.
Rather than succumb to the corporate doomsayers, the employees took a chance with their collective future and, with
October 2, 1987

last week's award, have proven to themselves and all of Canada that co-operation beats confrontation hands down.

Mr. Speaker, the export sale of commodities such as wheat, lumber, coal, uranium and potash is the backbone of the western Canadian economy. This reality is brought home each time a foreign Government adopts protectionist measures which inhibit the flow of Canadian goods.
Most recently, short-sighted American duties paralyzed the Saskatchewan potash industry. This is but one example of the damage that can be inflicted on our economy when there is no effective trade dispute settlement mechanism in place. If there exists the possibility of Canada and the United States agreeing to establish such a mechanism, if there is a way to ensure that Canadians will no longer be subject to the protectionist whims of the U.S. Congress, then the pursuit of such an agreement is worthy of a determined and committed effort on behalf of all Canadians.
I congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on his initiative and encourage him in pursuing every possible avenue to conclude a trade agreement with the U.S. that is both free and fair.

Mr. Speaker, over the last three years the Conservative Government has shown a reckless disregard for the security and safety of Canadian air travellers.
On June 25, 1985, two days after the Air-India tragedy, the then Minister of Transport, now the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), said: "Since these tragedies occurred the Government has moved quickly to ensure the security of Canadian air travellers." This week we learned from a Southam news story that airport guards missed 25 per cent of fake weapons carried through airport screening checks by federal Transport inspectors during a 15-month period. In effect this means our airports are only 75 per cent secure.
In April, 1986, again the Conservative Government of Canada announced plans to make our airports more secure. Notwithstanding those promises we find today that our airports are still not secure. Security is substandard. The Government's credibility on this issue is in tatters. Indeed, it
appears as though it does not know who is responsible for airport security.
On June 25, 1985, the Minister of Transport said: "Ultimate responsibility for flight security rests with the carriers." A document prepared for the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) dated September, 1985, says: "Airport and airline security in Canada is the responsibility of the Minister of Transport and is governed by regulations issued under the Aeronautics Act." That says that the Government does not understand who is responsible for airport security. Is it any wonder that Canadians feel so insecure when they travel on airlines in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, yesterday's call by Soviet Leader Mikhail Gorbachev for an Arctic zone of peace has much to recommend it and ought to be responded to by Canada. However, it is somewhat ironic that the appeal was made from Murmansk in the Kola Peninsula, one of the most heavily militarized areas in the world. This is the home base for the Delta IV and Typhoon Class Soviet submarines carrying SSN 20 and SSN 23 intercontinental nuclear missiles. These bases are of course heavily protected by naval and air defences.
If Gorbachev is really serious he could start the process by stopping the flights of AS 15 nuclear warhead-equipped Cruise missile-carrying Bear H strategic bombers over the Canadian Arctic. Canada can hardly be blamed for taking defensive measures against this blatant Soviet threat.

Mr. Speaker, every Standing Committee on Public Accounts of which I have been a member for the last eight years has recommended or supported intermittent reporting by the Auditor General as well as the single annual report presently required by law. Such a change in the Auditor General Act would allow much more current reporting to Parliament and increase the accountability of government, something we all desire.
Even as we have had all-Party agreement on the proposed change, the Government has consistently refused to allow Private Members' Bills on the subject to pass. Since that channel seems blocked, I call upon the Government to achieve the desired accountability by taking action itself on this important issue.

October 2, 1987
Oral Questions

maintopic: CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT, 1987 TRADE QUEBEC AS DISTINCT SOCIETY-POSITION OF LIBERAL PARTY
CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT, 1987 TRADE QUEBEC AS DISTINCT SOCIETY-POSITION OF LIBERAL PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
Canada as a country is unique because of its bilingualism and its multiculturalism. Canadians take great pride in the fact that this tremendous diversity does not prevent them from seeing themselves, first of all and above all, as profoundly Canadian.
However, refusing to admit that Quebec constitutes a distinct society, different from the rest of Canada, shows a complete lack of historical knowledge and a lack of respect for the Francophone population of Quebec. Unfortunately, that is what seems to be happening today the Liberal Caucus, where, according to one Caucus member, some fellow members are anti-Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, I am very disappointed in the narrow-minded attitude of those members of the Liberal Caucus who refuse to recognize the fact that Quebec is a distinct society. I am sad to hear that anti-Quebec forces are at work in the Liberal Party and in the Liberal Caucus in this House, forces that are casting doubts on the specific character of Quebec society.

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO ALL WHO PARTICIPATED IN DEVELOPMENT

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: TRIBUTE TO ALL WHO PARTICIPATED IN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Ottawa's Patro, one of Lowertown's most important Francophone institutions, will be celebrating its thirtieth anniversary tomorrow. As one of seven centres of this kind that exist in Eastern Canada, the Patro has, over the years, opened its doors to many children, teenagers and senior citizens, providing them with a place to play, to talk to friends or to go swimming. Throughout its history the Patro has made an admirable contribution to community development and it continues to do so today. Several times its very survival was in jeopardy. However, with the help of the people in the community, the leaders of Patro managed to meet the challenges facing them.
Thanks to the hard work and perseverance of members who have had to cope with all kinds of financial and other problems, tomorrow Patro will be celebrating its thirtieth anniversary. Those who take part in this great celebration will remember happy times spent in the pool, at fairs, festivals, day camps and summer camps, and the plays and many other activities that have been a source of entertainment for Ottawa's Lowertown, in my riding.
Today I wish to pay tribute to all those who, with Father David Lachance, the founder of the Saint-Vincent-Patro in Ottawa, have made this institution prosper. To all those who worked so hard, sincere thanks!

Mr. Speaker, the news that the bilateral trade negotiations may be back on the rails is good news for Canadians. It is time those who have opposed this historic negotiation got onside. The time for political rhetoric is over.
For the sake of Canada and the future of our young people and the new jobs a new deal would bring, opposition Members should stop trying to undermine the negotiations. Those opposite would have had us pull out months ago and subject us to further protectionist policies by our neighbour to the south. They have no solution to the problem, only selfish political posturing.
In the final hours it is time to end the scare tactics which have made some Canadians uneasy over the last several months, despite assurances from the Government that our social programs, the Auto Pact, agricultural marketing boards, and our cultural industries are not and have not been part of the bilateral negotiations. Those opposed have used these tactics to make cheap political gains.
As the talks enter the final stage let us pull together, and not give the U.S. the advantage of being divided. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has repeated from the beginning that if it is not in the interest of Canada there will be no deal. subtopic: FREE TRADE WITH UNITED STATES-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT ADHERE TO CONDITIONS
FREE TRADE WITH UNITED STATES-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT ADHERE TO CONDITIONS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):

The American position.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No fundamental change in the position we have put forward for some time. I think that is all that is appropriate for me to discuss at this stage.
However, I want to bring the House up to date with what happened since Question Period yesterday until today. During a meeting to consider the discussions that had been held yesterday in Washington, a telephone call was received from Secretary Baker, who is the Chairman of the U.S. Cabinet Committee directing their side of the discussions. On the basis of that telephone conversation, it became evident to us that we had reason to resume the negotiations. For that reason, the Minister of Finance and the Minister for International Trade, Ambassador Reisman and other of our technical experts are in Washington today.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is based upon that telephone conversation. As the Minister well understands, the deadline for the decision by the United States is Sunday night. We are now entering into negotiations in a two and one-half day period, for one of the most complex, difficult agreements ever arrived at between two countries.
Is it the position of both the Canadian and American Governments that in the two and one-half days they will have fully negotiated that agreement, or will the President of the
Oral Questions
United States announce on Sunday night simply some kind of vague agreement in principle which will, in effect, require Canada to make an agreement to a blank cheque without having had the opportunity to review its contents or whether in fact we agree with it?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs

Second, I cannot predict what will happen with these negotiations. They are in a more hopeful phase today then they have been at other times this week.
Third, with regard to the very valid point the Hon. Member makes about the complexity of the negotiations, he should bear in mind that precisely these issues have been under detailed consideration by the expert negotiators on both sides for a long number of months. We are not starting as though there were no past. There has been extensive preparation on the detail of these matters.
We will see if it will be possible, before the American deadline expires, to get the kinds of agreements on principle and on detail that would be necessary to serve Canada's interests. If we do, we will bring forward an agreement. If they do not serve Canada's interests, there will be no agreement.

Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: SOUTH AFRICA-VISIT BY BRITISH TRADE MISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no, 1 do not intend to protest the action because it is an action that is within the sovereign discretion of Great Britain. I have had extensive discussions, and the Hon. Member in his relations has had extensive discussions, with representatives of the British Parliament, and some members of the British Government. There is a different view on the effect of sanctions, and that difference is well known. They have a policy that differs from Canada's.
I guess what is most germane is how we can work together to ensure that the Commonwealth Conference, which opens in a couple of weeks in Vancouver, is a conference whose result will be to increase the pressures for change upon the Government of South Africa. That is what I am dedicated to doing.
Frankly, I do not think that we would advance our ability to do that by launching a condemnation of one of the principal members of the Commonwealth two weeks before the conference convenes.

My
question to the Secretary of State is this. Is it not about time that we stopped kowtowing to the British inclination to collusion with South Africa and go to the Commonwealth, exercising leadership to get from the Commonwealth, even if without the British, the kind of action in response to that apartheid-type regime that that civilized country and a civilized Commonwealth ought to be providing?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what is most important is for us to exert the maximum possible world pressure upon the South African regime to change the system of apartheid. That is what we have been doing consistently before the Nassau declaration, and with some effect.
The Hon. Member suggests that the Commonwealth should throw its weight absent Great Britain against South Africa. He knows that the Commonwealth economic weight absent Great Britain is absent a great deal. What would be most productive for us to do would be to find ways in which we can continue to work on the British to change their views about sanctions, but can also continue to work with them in areas where there is agreement to increase both the pressure for change on the South African Government and to increase the stability and security of the front-line states.
It is also, I think, possible for us to look at ways, with Britain and with other industrial countries that are not members of the Commonwealth, in which we can continue to add to pressures upon South Africa. That is the purpose of the policy of this Government.

subsubtopic: SUPERVISION OF PAROLEES IN METROPOLITAN TORONTO
speechtext:
On behalf of the Solicitor General, who is out of Ottawa today on official business, I am informed with respect to the allegations made by the Hon. Member that indeed there has been action taken with respect to improving the capacity of the Parole Board in the Toronto area. There has been a significant increase in the personnel operating out of the district of York in Toronto. The situation is well in hand.
The Solicitor General has responded quickly and effectively with respect to the workload that is facing the board in this part of the country.

Well, Mr. Speaker, that does not appear to be the case. The senior member of the National Parole Board had some very serious concerns with regard to parole supervision.

October 2, 1987
Oral Questions
The Solicitor General will know that it is a powder keg ready to explode. There are situations where dangerous inmates are not being properly supervised on the streets, and the public is at risk in Metropolitan Toronto.
The National Parole Board in Ontario has recommended a full review and audit to be made of the processes being followed, the staff problems, and reporting procedures.
I wish to ask the Government whether it is prepared to initiate that full review and audit, as recommended by the Senior Board Member of the National Parole Board in Ontario.
Good question.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to take issue with the inflammatory language used by the Hon. Member. It does not serve the system well to make that type of categorical catastrophic allegation. All of us are interested in ensuring that the system operates effectively on behalf of those it serves, and on behalf of the Canadian public.
1 have indicated that I am informed that the administration of the Parole Board in the Toronto area has been addressed by the Solicitor General when it has been brought to his attention. He is taking action to ensure that the best interests of our system of justice are addressed. I would simply counsel the Hon. Member not to make these statements, otherwise he will have his picture in the Toronto Sun.
Which page?
Page 3.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture. Would the Minister advise honey producers in Canada if a sulfathiazole certificate is necessary for shipments of honey to Japan and to European countries?
When will the Government certify more labs for testing honey?

Mr. Speaker, I believe that I answered part of that question yesterday. My hon. colleague should realize that product cannot move interprovincially unless it carries an export certificate issued by Agriculture Canada, and meets the standards established by the Department of National Health and Welfare. The same holds true for export product from Canada to the United States, and more recently to Japan.
What we are attempting to do is to negotiate with these two receiving countries an agreement that this product would be acceptable, providing that it carries with it an export certificate.
In order for us to issue the export certificate, it must meet the standards established by Health and Welfare.
